description: PollChat is an anonymous poll application that allows users to create polls and vote on them anonymously. With this nature of anonymity comes an obvious problem of bullying and harassment. This document walks through my thought process of investigating the app and retrieving user-inaccessible information.

text: The app had just launched and people from my school were already creating polls, but it was not long until I saw the first poll clearly made to slander someone. I became curious and started looking into what network traffic the app was sending and receiving. The authentication handling on the server side was poorly implemented. I was able to capture my own JWT token and started replicating and adjusting the API calls the app was making.

This is a simple API call - given the JWT token, the server responds with the user's full contacts list. When you first download the app, it requires access to your contacts to "verify" that you attend the school you selected. This information is stored on the server and can be retrieved with a single API call. So far, though, the data is protected behind proper authorization.
On the second day I still had not found a way to access other users' data, but I had found how the login flow worked. I was able to trigger the OTP generation endpoint for any phone number.

Digging deeper into the app's API calls, I noticed a separate authentication server at "auth.poll.chat". This server was less protected than the main API. I could send a six-digit one-time passcode to any phone number - registered or not - at one-minute intervals. The rate limiting on OTP generation was not the vulnerability I would be exploiting. The real issue was elsewhere.

Once a user sends themselves an OTP, they enter the code into the app's login page. The server responds with a JWT token granting full API access. The critical flaw: the server does not invalidate the login code after failed attempts, and the authentication endpoints have no rate limiting on login requests.

This means I could generate a login code for any phone number, then brute-force all one million possible six-digit combinations against the server with no penalty. The only unknown is whether a phone number actually has an account - a bad number wastes 20 to 120 minutes of guessing. I built a script that spawns five terminals, each covering a range of 200,000 codes, allowing me to exhaust all one million possibilities in under 30 minutes.
I will not be showcasing the sender.js file, but I assume you can imagine what it does.
